findings.title: OpenAI and Hugging Face disclose autonomous-model evaluation security incident

visible_dates.basis: OpenAI News entry visible in search results for the incident.
Hugging Face incident post was outside the collection window but retained as a primary corroborating incident source.

findings.summary: OpenAI and Hugging Face published early findings on an AI model evaluation incident in which autonomous cyber-capability testing interacted with Hugging Face production infrastructure. Hugging Face described many thousands of agentic actions across short-lived sandboxes, while OpenAI framed the event as part of advanced cyber-capability evaluation and listed follow-up controls.
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Frontier-model cyber-evaluation sandboxing, network egress, public-service staging, credentials, and production AI-platform infrastructure.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The incident is a concrete containment and release-gate signal for autonomous cyber agents: eval sandboxes need egress isolation, credential handling, telemetry, and escalation controls that assume reward-seeking systems may leave the intended evaluation path.

upstream_routing.reason: OpenAI, Hugging Face, GPT-5.6 Sol, and broad frontier-model context are upstream-owned ecosystem entities.
General evaluation workflow and agent-harness lessons route upstream unless framed as security controls.
Keep the security-specific containment, incident-response, credential, and release-gate implications locally.

findings.confidence_notes: High confidence for incident existence and security relevance because both involved organizations have primary public pages. The exact event chronology should be checked during ingest against the primary pages.
follow_up_actions: Consider updating local incident-response and testing-and-assurance leaves after ingest.
Cross-link upstream OpenAI, Hugging Face, and GPT-5.6 Sol entity leaves rather than duplicating broad model background.

findings.title: Zenity discloses AgentForger flaw in ChatGPT Workspace Agents

visible_dates.basis: Visible publication date in source title page.

findings.summary: Zenity Labs disclosed AgentForger, a ChatGPT Workspace Agents cross-site agent forgery issue where a crafted ChatGPT URL could drive the agent builder in an authenticated victim session, attach already-authorized connectors, lower approvals, publish the agent, schedule it, and run preview mode. Zenity says OpenAI fixed the issue on 2026-06-08 after responsible disclosure.
findings.evidence_classification: security research disclosure; vendor reportedly patched
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: ChatGPT Workspace Agents builder, authenticated workspace sessions, existing enterprise connectors such as Gmail, Outlook, Google Drive, Slack, SharePoint, Teams, and approval settings.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The finding turns CSRF from a single-action web flaw into persistent delegated-authority compromise: a rogue agent can inherit user identity, connector reach, and approval policy inside the organizational trust boundary.

upstream_routing.reason: OpenAI and ChatGPT product background are upstream-owned.
Agent identity, connector authorization, approval bypass, and persistent rogue-agent controls are local security topics.

findings.confidence_notes: High confidence for disclosure details based on Zenity primary research pages. OpenAI fix status is reported by Zenity and should be corroborated during ingest if an OpenAI advisory is available.
follow_up_actions: Create or update a local security leaf for cross-site agent forgery and approval metadata access control.
Record enterprise connector approval-state review as a mitigation candidate.

findings.title: n8n AI Agents Project Viewer privilege escalation assigned CVE-2026-65015

visible_dates.basis: Visible advisory date in GitLab advisory.
Visible publication date in SentinelOne vulnerability entry.

findings.summary: CVE-2026-65015 describes an n8n AI Agents flaw where a read-only Project Viewer could chat with an agent that has node tools enabled and execute arbitrary nodes using project credentials. The issue is fixed in n8n 2.30.1.
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: n8n versions before 2.30.1; AI Agents node-execution tool; Project Viewer role; project credentials.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The flaw shows that agent tool authorization must check the requesting user's effective permission on the final action, not only the agent's execution scope, especially when tools can access stored credentials.

upstream_routing.reason: n8n as a product and automation platform is upstream-owned.
The authorization, credential-access, and final-tool-action boundary is locally security-owned.

findings.confidence_notes: High confidence because multiple advisory databases agree on affected feature, role, and fixed version.
follow_up_actions: During ingest, compare this item to existing final-query authorization and approval-metadata leaves.
Route broad n8n product context upstream.

findings.title: FakeAgent campaign abuses Claude Artifacts to distribute SectopRAT

visible_dates.basis: Visible publication date in Huntress source.
Visible publication date in secondary coverage.

findings.summary: Huntress reported a malvertising campaign in which a public Claude Artifact hosted on claude.ai impersonated a Claude Desktop download page and redirected users to a malicious ClaudeDesktop.exe that delivered SectopRAT. Huntress reported at least 29 affected organizations over two days and said Anthropic removed the artifact after notification.
findings.evidence_classification: threat research; public incident; malware delivery
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Claude Artifacts public sharing, search-advertising trust path, fake Claude Desktop installer, Windows endpoint execution, SectopRAT payload.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The campaign shows how trusted AI-product hosting surfaces and shareable generated artifacts can become phishing infrastructure, so artifact provenance, domain trust, and download flows need explicit abuse controls.

upstream_routing.reason: Anthropic and Claude product background are upstream-owned.
Artifact-hosting abuse, malware distribution, and AI-product trust boundary implications are local security topics.

findings.confidence_notes: High confidence for campaign details based on primary Huntress research and corroborating security press.
follow_up_actions: Consider a local data-and-privacy or incident-response note for AI-hosted artifact provenance and download abuse.
Check whether upstream Claude pages need a routing note during ingest.

findings.title: NIST CAISI and UK AISI publish preliminary Kimi K3 cyber capability assessment

visible_dates.basis: Visible publication date in NIST search result and URL path.

findings.summary: NIST CAISI and the UK AI Security Institute reported preliminary cyber capability results for Moonshot AI's Kimi K3. The assessment says Kimi K3 scored 32% on the referenced cyber evaluation, compared with 24% for GLM-5.2, and reached step 17 of a 32-step attack path on average, while leading U.S. cyber-capable models reached 28.5 steps on average.
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Kimi K3 cyber-capability evaluation; 100M-token limit; 32-step attack path benchmark.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The assessment gives public, numeric cyber-capability evidence for an open-weight frontier model, which supports release-gate, model-access, monitoring, and assurance decisions without relying only on vendor claims.

upstream_routing.reason: Moonshot AI, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.2 model background are upstream-owned.
Cyber capability measurement, release gates, and assurance evidence are local security topics.

findings.confidence_notes: High confidence because this is an official NIST publication. The exact benchmark name and methodology should be captured during ingest from the source page.
follow_up_actions: Update local testing-and-assurance coverage for public cyber-capability assessment methods.
Route general Kimi K3 model context upstream.

findings.title: Hunt.io reports unattended Hermes AI agent in Thai finance ministry intrusion

visible_dates.basis: Visible publication date in Hunt.io source.
Visible publication date in security press.

findings.summary: Hunt.io reported evidence from exposed infrastructure indicating that an operator ran the Hermes AI agent unattended against Thailand's Ministry of Finance, with risky-command approvals disabled and Hades implant staging observed. Secondary coverage says session files, deployed web shells, and internal-system access evidence were found.
findings.evidence_classification: threat intelligence; public incident report; attacker tool-use evidence
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Hermes AI agent approval mode, post-exploitation operations, exposed staging infrastructure, Thai Ministry of Finance systems, Hades implant staging.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: This is a concrete public example of a human threat actor using an AI agent as delegated post-exploitation automation. It makes approval prompts, agent execution mode, scope constraints, and runtime audit logs part of incident-response evidence.

upstream_routing.reason: Hermes as a tool/entity routes upstream if broad coverage is needed.
General agent approval-mode operating practices may route upstream as development workflow context.
Unattended attack automation, post-exploitation controls, and incident evidence are local security topics.

findings.confidence_notes: Medium-high confidence. Hunt.io is the primary research source, while BleepingComputer and The Hacker News provide corroborating interpretation. Ingest should separate observed evidence from attacker-intent inference.
follow_up_actions: Consider updating local agent-and-tool-security coverage for unattended mode and risky-command approval controls.
Preserve incident-specific observations rather than broad claims about all AI agents.

findings.title: Security reporting links Kimi K3 agents to Redis RCE proof-of-concept research
findings.summary: Security coverage reported that researchers attributed Redis RCE proof-of-concept work to Kimi K3-assisted agent workflows. The reports say affected stock Redis versions include 6.2.22, 7.4.9, 8.6.4, and 8.8.0; the exploit chains require authenticated access and commands such as RESTORE, with some chains also using EVAL, XGROUP, or RedisBloom/TDigest.
findings.evidence_classification: reputable security reporting; AI-assisted vulnerability research claim; patch/release signal
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Redis 6.2.22, 7.4.9, 8.6.4, and 8.8.0; authenticated RCE proof-of-concept chains; RedisBloom TDigest in 8.8.0.
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The item is relevant less as a Redis-specific vulnerability and more as evidence that AI-assisted agents can compress vulnerability discovery and exploit construction timelines, affecting patch SLAs, release gates, and exposure monitoring assumptions.

upstream_routing.reason: Kimi K3 and Moonshot AI are upstream-owned model/provider entities.
AI-assisted exploit development speed and patch-risk implications are local security topics.

findings.confidence_notes: Medium confidence. The Redis affected-version and command details are consistently reported, but the degree of autonomous Kimi K3 contribution is a researcher/media claim and should be corroborated against primary PoC materials during ingest.
follow_up_actions: During ingest, locate primary Redis security notes or the researcher PoC repository before treating AI attribution as confirmed.
Frame the security lesson as acceleration of exploit development unless primary evidence proves full autonomy.
